clue.text: They might be occupied in form-filling

definitions.text: They might be occupied in form-filling

parts.words: They might be occupied in form-filling
parts.note: reads like paperwork, but a form is a school class, and filling it means pupils sitting at their places

explanation.surface: Someone muses on what people are busy with while completing official paperwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form-filling' suggests bureaucracy; in British schools a form is a class, and a full classroom has every pupil's writing table taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Pupils in a school class each occupy a writing table, so these items are what a filled form sits at.

clue.text: A piece of furniture set up on board ? Doubtful

indicators.note: in a down entry, set up means raised from bottom to top, so the furniture word is read upwards

parts.note: a bed is a piece of furniture
a board is a table, as in board and lodging

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether an item of furniture can be put up aboard a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' reverses BED to DEB in this down entry; 'on' places it above A TABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something open to argument and uncertain is doubtful.

clue.text: Pelt sometimes needs dressing

definitions.meaning: to pelt is to throw missiles at, as rocks at a target
building rock is often dressed, cut and smoothed by a mason before use

explanation.surface: An animal skin sometimes has to be treated before it can be used.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pelt' looks like an animal's skin, but it is the verb: to throw rocks at.
explanation.definitionFit: To pelt with rocks is to hurl them at someone, and masons dress, or shape, quarried rock.

clue.text: Fish seen rising by carrier of line

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means going upwards, so the fish are read from bottom to top

parts.note: eels are fish
per means by, as in per post

explanation.surface: Fish are observed coming up beside a fisherman's line.
explanation.walkthrough: In British railway usage, the wooden or concrete beam under the rails is the support for the track, the 'line'.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway tie, in British usage, is the beam that carries the rails of the line.

clue.text: Oust about one petitioner

indicators.note: about means placed around, so the word for oust wraps the other piece

parts.note: to oust is to supplant, take another's place
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A humble petitioner is thrown out of somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: A suppliant is one who humbly begs or makes a petition, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Formality in church after leading 10, perhaps

indicators.note: after means the church abbreviation follows the other piece

parts.note: 10 across is an actor, and the leading actor in a production is the star

explanation.surface: Rigid formality reigns in a church following the lead actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Starch, figuratively, is a stiff, formal manner, like starched linen.

clue.text: I slug it quietly out with my opponent

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical direction for quietly

indicators.note: out signals the words are knocked out of shape and rearranged

explanation.surface: A fighter describes trading blows with an opponent without making a fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges I SLUG IT into UGILIST, after P from 'quietly'; the speaker's opponent in a slugging match is a boxer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone I slug it out with in the ring is a boxer, so my opponent is a fighter.

clue.text: Creditor holds, note of drowned Greek

indicators.note: holds means contains, so the creditor word grips the note inside it

parts.note: a creditor is a lender
A is a musical note

explanation.surface: A creditor keeps a record of a Greek who drowned.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth, Leander swam the Hellespont nightly to visit Hero and drowned in a storm.
explanation.definitionFit: Leander of Greek legend drowned swimming the Hellespont to reach his lover Hero.

clue.text: Animals seen before a rest-break

parts.note: ante is Latin for before

indicators.note: break means smashed apart, so the letters of rest are rearranged

explanation.surface: Animals are spotted ahead of a pause in the work.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen joins 'rest' and 'break' as if a pause; 'break' rearranges REST to TERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Anteaters are toothless mammals that feed on ants and termites.

clue.text: " —— of London … —— of life " (Johnson)

parts.note: fill the gaps in Samuel Johnson's saying that a man who is weary of London is weary of life

explanation.surface: A famous quotation from Dr Johnson with two words missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Johnson's saying is 'When a man is tired of London, he is tired of life'; the same word fills both gaps.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in Johnson's line means weary, as in having had enough.

clue.text: Missile Moore repaired appears in report

indicators.note: the rearranged name sits inside the word for report, appearing within it

parts.note: a report is a loud noise such as a bang from a gun

indicators.note: something repaired is put back together differently, so the letters of the name are reworked

explanation.surface: A man called Moore has fixed a missile, and the news shows up in a report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'report' looks like the news, but it is the bang of a gun; 'repaired' rearranges the name to OOMER and 'appears in' sets it inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The Australian curved throwing stick is a hunting weapon hurled at a target, a kind of missile.

clue.text: Some refractory employee in the Strand ?

indicators.note: some of the word is taken, signalling letters lifted from inside refractory

explanation.surface: A stubborn worker is causing trouble in a central London street.
explanation.walkthrough: The Strand is a London street lined with theatres, so a person employed there is a stage performer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Strand is in London's theatreland, so someone working there is a stage player.

clue.text: Musicians spotted by Conan Doyle ?

parts.note: a group of players covered in spots, read as the title of a Sherlock Holmes story written by the author

explanation.surface: The creator of Sherlock Holmes catches sight of a group of musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' looks like 'seen', but it means dotted with marks, giving a dotted group of musicians, which is the title of one of Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes stories.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the title of an 1892 Sherlock Holmes short story by Arthur Conan Doyle.

clue.text: Humphrey's picturesque graffiti ?

parts.note: graffiti scrawled on a lavatory wall is jokingly called toilet art, and a famous Humphrey of Hollywood bore that sound as his surname

explanation.surface: Someone named Humphrey has daubed colourful graffiti somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Bog is British slang for a toilet, so lavatory-wall graffiti is bog art; Humphrey Bogart was the Hollywood star of Casablanca.
explanation.definitionFit: Humphrey Bogart was the film actor, and his surname splits into slang for toilet plus a word for pictures.

clue.text: People added to the time of a local call

definitions.text: People added to the time of a local call

parts.words: People added to the time of a local call
parts.note: a local is a pub, and the landlord's closing call is time followed by an address to the drinkers

explanation.surface: Someone is told the extra people added to the cost of a local phone call.
explanation.walkthrough: 'local call' suggests the telephone; a local is a British pub, where the closing cry is 'Time, gentlemen, please!'
explanation.definitionFit: The pub landlord calls 'Time, gentlemen, please', so the men addressed are those added to the word time.

clue.text: Tureen is upset, leaving us hungry

indicators.note: a soup dish that is upset is knocked over, so its letters, with is, are jumbled

explanation.surface: A soup dish has been knocked over, so there's nothing left for us to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: Esurient is a literary word meaning greedy or ravenous, a synonym of hungry.

clue.text: Ability to endure the sort of claret one supplied ?

indicators.note: sort of hints at a rough version, so the letters of claret one are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone's capacity to stand a particular wine that has been provided.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolerance is the capacity to put up with something unpleasant.

clue.text: Late Bisley winner ?

parts.note: late reads as deceased, and a winner at the rifle meeting would be a crack marksman

explanation.surface: A tribute to a champion of the shooting competition who has died.
explanation.walkthrough: Bisley, in Surrey, is home to Britain's National Rifle Association shooting championships; 'late' means dead.
explanation.definitionFit: An unerring marksman is called this, and a deceased one is literally late.

clue.text: Retired French nursemaid was first to be honoured

indicators.note: retired means drawn back, so the French word is read backwards

parts.note: bonne is French for a maid or nursemaid
to be first is to lead, so was first gives led

explanation.surface: A French nanny who has retired was the first to receive an honour.
explanation.definitionFit: To be ennobled is to be raised to the peerage, a great honour.

clue.text: Top lawyer we hear from Aberdeen ?

definitions.meaning: the leading barrister, king of the legal bar
an Aberdeen terrier is a dog, and what we hear from a dog is its noise

explanation.surface: We are told about a leading lawyer from the Scottish city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aberdeen' looks like the city, but it is the Aberdeen (Scottish) terrier; 'hear' looks like a homophone signal but is plain listening.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog's yapping is what a terrier makes, and the top of the Bar would be its king.

clue.text: That creature in the pop number ?

definitions.text: That creature in the pop number ?

parts.words: That creature in the pop number ?
parts.note: a pop number looks like a chart hit, but it is the nursery song whose refrain says the animal goes pop

explanation.surface: Someone asks which animal is mentioned in a hit song.
explanation.walkthrough: The old song 'Pop Goes the Weasel' is the 'pop number', not a modern chart hit.
explanation.definitionFit: The animal named in the traditional rhyme 'Pop Goes the Weasel' is this small carnivore.

clue.text: Is wrong about sea-trip needed by typists

indicators.note: about means placed around, so the word for is wrong encloses the other piece

parts.note: errs means is wrong

indicators.note: trip means stumble, so the letters of sea fall into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is mistaken about a voyage needed by office workers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sea-trip' reads as a cruise, but 'trip' is the anagram signal, making ASE, which 'about' puts inside the word for 'Is wrong'.
explanation.definitionFit: Typists once used rubbers to correct mistakes on typed pages.

clue.text: It's not " really" played on grass

definitions.text: It's not " really" played on grass

parts.words: It's not " really" played on grass
parts.note: the original indoor court game is called real; the version not called real is the one played on lawns

explanation.surface: Someone claims a game isn't truly played on a lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: Real tennis is the old indoor game; lawn tennis is the one that is 'not real' and played on grass, as at Wimbledon.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawn tennis, unlike real tennis, is played outdoors on grass courts.

clue.text: Composer made the Elliot Gay record

indicators.note: made here means fashioned into something new, so the letters of the three words are worked into the name

explanation.surface: Someone called Elliot Gay has made a record, and it turns out to be a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made' rearranges ELLIOT GAY RECORD into the composer's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Coleridge-Taylor was the English composer of Hiawatha's Wedding Feast.

clue.text: The object of tossing up in games

definitions.text: The object of tossing up in games

parts.words: The object of tossing up in games
parts.note: tossing up looks like flipping a coin, but at Highland games a heavy pole is thrown end over end

explanation.surface: Someone asks what the coin toss at the start of a match is for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tossing up' suggests a coin toss; at Scottish Highland games competitors throw a tree trunk.
explanation.definitionFit: This long wooden pole is thrown end over end at Scottish Highland games.

clue.text: Political scientist in a silk combine

indicators.note: combine means mix together, so the letters of a silk are rearranged

explanation.surface: A political theorist is dressed in a blended silk outfit.
explanation.definitionFit: Harold Laski was a British political theorist at the London School of Economics.

clue.text: Disney work is one written by degrees

parts.note: a BA is a Bachelor of Arts degree
an MB is a Bachelor of Medicine degree
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A Disney film is said to have been written by someone with university qualifications.
explanation.walkthrough: 'degrees' supplies two university qualifications in a row, the arts one then the medical one, and 'written by' sets the numeral after them.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1942 animated film about a young deer was made by Walt Disney's studio.

clue.text: Mother's boy about to finish as Labour statesman

indicators.note: about means going around, so the phrase for a mother's boy surrounds the other piece

parts.note: a mother's boy is her son
to finish is to end

explanation.surface: A man devoted to his mother is about to bring a Labour politician's career to a close.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Henderson was a British Labour Party leader, Foreign Secretary and Nobel Peace Prize winner.

clue.text: Old characters carry a gun. They're vagabonds

indicators.note: to carry is to hold within, so the old letters contain the other pieces

parts.note: runes are the characters of ancient Germanic alphabets
gat is old slang for a gun

explanation.surface: Ancient scripts are said to bear arms, and the people carrying them are tramps.
explanation.definitionFit: Runagate is an old word for a wanderer, fugitive or tramp, so the plural matches vagabonds.

clue.text: Strike caused by singularly bad beer ?

definitions.meaning: an old slang word for weak or poor beer is plural; taken in the singular it gives this word

explanation.surface: A walkout was sparked by a single dreadful pint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swipes' was old slang for thin, poor-quality beer; 'singularly' tells you to drop the plural ending.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweeping hit is a blow, while thin weak ale was once called by this name in the plural.
